entries.meaning: The contraction of I have, the auxiliary of the present perfect. ---
examples: I've lived in Chicago since 2015.
I've already eaten, thanks.
I've got to leave by six.
entries.русский: я уже (сделал) — сокращение от I have
entries.type: have — a subject plus the auxiliary have
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: 've contracts the auxiliary only. American English does not contract have meaning 'own': I have a car, never ✗ I've a car (that is British and dated). And no contraction can end a clause: Yes, I have, never ✗ Yes, I've.

entries.meaning: The contraction of you have, the auxiliary of the present perfect. ---
examples: You've been working too hard lately.
You've got mail.
If you've finished the form, bring it to the window.
entries.русский: ты/вы уже (сделал) — сокращение от you have
entries.type: have — a subject plus the auxiliary have
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
entries.contrast: Unstressed, you've is said /jəv/ and the 've is easy to miss: You've seen it and You saw it differ by one weak syllable. The written trap is the pronoun — you've is you have, you're is you are, and your is the possessive.

entries.meaning: The contraction of we have, the auxiliary of the present perfect. ---
examples: We've known each other since college.
We've got a problem with the heater.
We've never been to Texas.
entries.русский: мы уже (сделали) — сокращение от we have
entries.type: have — a subject plus the auxiliary have
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
entries.contrast: We've is pronounced exactly like weave. Do not confuse it with we'd (we would or we had) or we're (we are).

entries.meaning: The contraction of they have, the auxiliary of the present perfect. ---
examples: They've lived in that house for thirty years.
They've already left for the airport.
I don't think they've met before.
entries.русский: они уже (сделали) — сокращение от they have
entries.type: have — a subject plus the auxiliary have
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
entries.contrast: The three they contractions are different words: they're is they are, they'd is they would or they had, and they've is they have. None of them is their.

examples: Students who've missed three classes can't take the final.
There are plenty of people who've never heard of him.
Who've you been talking to?
entries.русский: которые уже (сделали) — сокращение от who have
entries.type: have — the relative or question word who plus the auxiliary have
entries.register: standard — but far rarer than who's, and mostly heard rather than written
entries.question form: Who've you told? is normal in speech; in writing most Americans spell it out — Who have you told?
entries.contrast: Who've is who have; who's is who is or who has; whose is the possessive and takes no apostrophe.

entries.meaning: The contraction of could have: what was possible but did not happen. ---
examples: You could've told me you were bringing someone.
The whole thing could've been avoided.
I could've sworn I left my keys on the table.
entries.русский: мог бы (тогда) — сокращение от could have
entries.type: modal — could plus a contracted have
entries.register: informal — normal in speech; formal writing spells it out as could have
entries.question form: There is no contracted question: Could you have known?, never ✗ Could've you known?
entries.contrast: The -'ve is unstressed /əv/ and sounds exactly like of, which is why ✗ could of is the most common spelling error in written American English. It is never correct, in any register — if you cannot hear which it is, expand it to could have.

entries.meaning: The contraction of would have: what was going to be true but was not. ---
examples: I would've called, but my phone was dead.
She would've made a great teacher.
Nobody would've guessed he was nervous.
entries.русский: сделал бы (тогда) — сокращение от would have
entries.type: modal — would plus a contracted have
entries.register: informal — normal in speech; formal writing spells it out as would have
entries.question form: There is no contracted question: Would you have come?, never ✗ Would've you come?
entries.contrast: ✗ would of is never correct — the -'ve is unstressed /əv/ and only sounds like of. Watch the halves of the third conditional: If I'd known, I would've called — had in the if clause, would have in the main clause, never ✗ If I would've known.

entries.meaning: The contraction of should have: what was the right thing to do and was not done. ---
examples: I should've studied more for that test.
You should've seen the look on his face.
We should've left an hour ago.
entries.русский: надо было (сделать) — сокращение от should have
entries.type: modal — should plus a contracted have
entries.register: informal — normal in speech; formal writing spells it out as should have
entries.question form: There is no contracted question: Should I have said something?, never ✗ Should've I said something?
entries.contrast: ✗ should of is never correct, however much the -'ve sounds like of. Note what the form means: should've is always a reproach or a regret about the past — You should've called says that you did not call.

entries.meaning: The contraction of might have: a guess about the past, or about what nearly happened. ---
examples: He might've left already — his car is gone.
I might've put it in the other drawer.
You might've warned me before I signed it.
entries.русский: возможно, сделал — сокращение от might have
entries.type: modal — might plus a contracted have
entries.register: informal — normal in speech; formal writing spells it out as might have
entries.contrast: ✗ might of is never correct. Keep the two deductions apart: might've is a guess (He might've left — maybe, maybe not), while must've is a conclusion (He must've left — I am sure of it).

entries.meaning: The contraction of must have: a confident conclusion about the past. ---
examples: He must've left — the lights are off.
You must've been exhausted after that drive.
I must've missed the turn somewhere.
entries.русский: наверняка сделал — сокращение от must have
entries.type: modal — must plus a contracted have
entries.register: informal — normal in speech; formal writing spells it out as must have
entries.contrast: ✗ must of is never correct. And must've is never obligation in the past: He must've left means 'I am sure he left'; for obligation you say he had to leave.

examples: I'd love to come to the party.
I'd rather stay home tonight.
If I had the money, I'd buy it.
By the time she called, I'd already gone to bed.
I'd never seen snow before that winter.
I'd better get going.

senses.head: The contraction of I would
examples: I'd love to come to the party.
I'd rather stay home tonight.
If I had the money, I'd buy it.

senses.head: The contraction of I had, the auxiliary of the past perfect
examples: By the time she called, I'd already gone to bed.
I'd never seen snow before that winter.
I'd better get going.

entries.русский: я бы; я уже — сокращение от I would или I had
entries.type: would — or had; the verb that follows tells you which
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
entries.ambiguity: I'd is I would before a bare verb (I'd go) and I had before a past participle (I'd gone). Two fixed phrases settle it by themselves: I'd better is always had, I'd rather is always would.
entries.contrast: The third conditional uses both in one sentence: If I'd known, I'd have said something — the first I'd is had, the second is would.

examples: You'd like her — everybody does.
You'd be surprised how often that happens.
If you asked him, you'd get the same answer.
You'd better call your mother.
She said you'd already paid for the tickets.
By then you'd been waiting almost an hour.

senses.head: The contraction of you would
examples: You'd like her — everybody does.
You'd be surprised how often that happens.
If you asked him, you'd get the same answer.

senses.head: The contraction of you had, the auxiliary of the past perfect
examples: You'd better call your mother.
She said you'd already paid for the tickets.
By then you'd been waiting almost an hour.

entries.русский: ты бы; ты уже — сокращение от you would или you had
entries.type: would — or had; the verb that follows tells you which
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
entries.ambiguity: You'd like it is would; You'd finished is had. You'd better is had — and in speech it shrinks further, to you better or even a bare better.
entries.contrast: You'd is you would or you had, never you are — that is you're.

examples: He'd never admit it, but he was scared.
I asked if he'd help us move.
He'd rather walk than wait for the bus.
By the time we got there, he'd eaten.
She told me he'd been sick all week.
He'd better have a good excuse.

senses.head: The contraction of he would
examples: He'd never admit it, but he was scared.
I asked if he'd help us move.
He'd rather walk than wait for the bus.

senses.head: The contraction of he had, the auxiliary of the past perfect
examples: By the time we got there, he'd eaten.
She told me he'd been sick all week.
He'd better have a good excuse.

entries.русский: он бы; он уже — сокращение от he would или he had
entries.type: would — or had; the verb that follows tells you which
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
entries.ambiguity: He'd go is would; He'd gone is had. He'd better is had, he'd rather is would.
entries.contrast: He'd is a homophone of heed, and in the middle of a sentence the h often drops, so what he'd said runs together as one word. Do not confuse it with he's, which is he is or he has.

examples: She'd like to meet you sometime.
She'd rather not talk about it.
I knew she'd say no.
She'd already left when I got there.
She'd never flown before that trip.
He mentioned that she'd been promoted twice.

senses.head: The contraction of she would
examples: She'd like to meet you sometime.
She'd rather not talk about it.
I knew she'd say no.

senses.head: The contraction of she had, the auxiliary of the past perfect
examples: She'd already left when I got there.
She'd never flown before that trip.
He mentioned that she'd been promoted twice.

entries.русский: она бы; она уже — сокращение от she would или she had
entries.type: would — or had; the verb that follows tells you which
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
entries.ambiguity: She'd like it is would; She'd liked it is had. The participle is the whole test: she'd take it (would) against she'd taken it (had).
entries.contrast: She'd is she would or she had, never she is or she has — those are she's.

examples: It'd be great if you could come.
It'd take about two hours to drive there.
I thought it'd be colder than this.
The ground was soaked — it'd rained all night.
By morning it'd stopped snowing.

senses.head: The contraction of it would
examples: It'd be great if you could come.
It'd take about two hours to drive there.
I thought it'd be colder than this.

senses.head: The contraction of it had, the auxiliary of the past perfect
examples: The ground was soaked — it'd rained all night.
By morning it'd stopped snowing.

entries.русский: это было бы; это уже — сокращение от it would или it had
entries.type: would — or had, though the had reading is rare
entries.register: informal — common in speech, seldom written outside dialogue; in print, spell out it would
entries.ambiguity: It'd take an hour is would; It'd rained all night is had. With it, the would reading is far commoner.
entries.contrast: Unlike the one-syllable it's, it'd has two syllables, and the American flapped t makes it sound close to 'id-ud'. It is a spoken form: write it would.

examples: We'd love to have you over for dinner.
We'd rather leave before the traffic starts.
If it were cheaper, we'd buy it.
We'd already eaten by the time she showed up.
They told us we'd missed the deadline.
We'd better hurry.

senses.head: The contraction of we would
examples: We'd love to have you over for dinner.
We'd rather leave before the traffic starts.
If it were cheaper, we'd buy it.

senses.head: The contraction of we had, the auxiliary of the past perfect
examples: We'd already eaten by the time she showed up.
They told us we'd missed the deadline.
We'd better hurry.

entries.русский: мы бы; мы уже — сокращение от we would или we had
entries.type: would — or had; the verb that follows tells you which
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
entries.ambiguity: We'd go is would; We'd gone is had. We'd better is had, we'd rather is would.
entries.contrast: We'd sounds exactly like weed. Keep it apart from we've (we have) and we're (we are).

examples: They'd never agree to that.
I figured they'd call back by now.
They'd rather pay cash.
They'd already sold the house when we called.
She said they'd been friends since high school.

senses.head: The contraction of they would
examples: They'd never agree to that.
I figured they'd call back by now.
They'd rather pay cash.

senses.head: The contraction of they had, the auxiliary of the past perfect
examples: They'd already sold the house when we called.
She said they'd been friends since high school.

entries.русский: они бы; они уже — сокращение от they would или they had
entries.type: would — or had; the verb that follows tells you which
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
entries.ambiguity: They'd agree is would; They'd agreed is had — and here the two differ by one consonant, so listen for the -ed.
entries.contrast: They'd is they would or they had; they've is they have; they're is they are; their and there are not contractions at all.

examples: There'd be a lot less traffic if we left at six.
Nobody warned us there'd be a fee.
If we canceled now, there'd be no refund.
There'd been a fire in the building the week before.
She had no idea there'd been any complaints.

senses.head: The contraction of there would
examples: There'd be a lot less traffic if we left at six.
Nobody warned us there'd be a fee.
If we canceled now, there'd be no refund.

senses.head: The contraction of there had, always before been
examples: There'd been a fire in the building the week before.
She had no idea there'd been any complaints.

entries.русский: было бы; уже было — сокращение от there would или there had
entries.type: would — or had; with the existential there
entries.register: standard — much commoner in speech than in writing
entries.ambiguity: There'd be trouble is would; There'd been trouble is had. After there, the had reading is always followed by been.
entries.contrast: This is the existential there of there is and there was, not the place word — and never their or they're.

examples: Who'd have thought it would end like that?
Who'd want to drive four hours for one meeting?
The witness who'd seen the car never came forward.
He introduced me to a cousin who'd just moved to town.

senses.head: The contraction of who would
examples: Who'd have thought it would end like that?
Who'd want to drive four hours for one meeting?

senses.head: The contraction of who had, the auxiliary of the past perfect
examples: The witness who'd seen the car never came forward.
He introduced me to a cousin who'd just moved to town.

entries.русский: кто бы; который уже — сокращение от who would или who had
entries.type: would — or had; the verb that follows tells you which
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
entries.ambiguity: Who'd want that? is would; the man who'd left is had. Casual speech adds a third reading that is never written outside dialogue: Who'd you call? is who did.
entries.contrast: Who'd is a homophone of hood. It is not who's (who is or who has), and not whose, the possessive, which takes no apostrophe.

examples: That'd be great, thanks.
That'd cost more than the car is worth.
I didn't think that'd work.
He said that'd already been decided.
We assumed that'd been taken care of.

senses.head: The contraction of that would
examples: That'd be great, thanks.
That'd cost more than the car is worth.
I didn't think that'd work.

senses.head: The contraction of that had, the auxiliary of the past perfect
examples: He said that'd already been decided.
We assumed that'd been taken care of.

entries.русский: это было бы — сокращение от that would или that had
entries.type: would — or had, though the had reading is rare
entries.register: informal — speech and dialogue only; in writing, spell out that would
entries.ambiguity: That'd be great is would; that'd been settled is had. With that, 'd is almost always would.
entries.contrast: Two syllables, with the American flapped t, so it sounds close to 'thad-ud'. It is not that's, which is that is or that has.
